about: Generated by papers/p1/build.mjs from atom/js/table.js; do not edit. Each claim's value is recomputed from the bake on every build.

claims.claim: Gauss's law in 4D (a 1/r² potential) has no atom: below a critical strength nothing binds, above it the ground state falls to the centre, its energy set by wherever the calculation stops (no Bohr radius either way)
claims.value: α = 0.45: bound on no grid; α = 0.7: ε = -5.875e+3, -5.872e+5, -5.870e+7 hartree for r₀ = 10⁻³, 10⁻⁴, 10⁻⁵ (×9.99e+3 over 10⁻² in r₀: ε ∝ 1/r₀²); the critical strength is ½ (Hardy's inequality in 4D)

claims.claim: Among power laws 1/r^η only η = 1 keeps a shell's levels together (2s with 2p, 3s with 3d), the degeneracy that makes shells of 2(l + 1)² and rows of 2, 10, 10, 28 …
Pinned in 4D, 1/r isn't harmonic: ∇²(1/r) = −1/r³ in empty space, so there is no Gauss's law for it
… and no shell theorem: a shell of charge is felt at its own radius at k(1) = 8/3π of a point charge's pull, and a hollow conductor's centre sits at 3π/8 of its wall's potential (no Faraday cage)

Atoms don't collapse: total energies follow each world's Thomas–Fermi law, Z^(3−2/D) (Z^(5/2) in four dimensions, Z^(7/3) in ours), as the shell theorem's absence would have to break if matter were unstable
claims.value: fitted exponent 2.527 over Z = 10–140 in 4D (5/2 = 2.5); 2.387 over Z = 10–36 in ours (7/3 = 2.333); both a little above, as finite-Z corrections make them

claims.claim: The 4D table's rows hold 2, 10, 10, 28, 28, 60 elements: the rows Négadi and Kibler's generalized Madelung rule (stated for any D, worked out by them for D = 2) gives when applied to D = 4
claims.value: solved 2, 10, 10, 28, 28, 60 (and 2 of the next by Z = 140); the rule 2, 10, 10, 28, 28, 60

claims.claim: Inside the rows, read as a ground-configuration rule (which, like Madelung's in ours, it isn't meant to be exactly): most 4D atoms fill exactly in its order, and every other moves one or two electrons between two subshells, nearly always from an outer s into the d or f below it, as our chromium and copper do

The +2 and +3 ions, each searched for its own ground state: ours' second and third ionizations agree with NIST more closely than the first; in 4D the 3d row's ions lose their outer s electrons first, as ours do, while the first elements of the 4d and 5d blocks give up a d electron first at +1 or +2, as our yttrium and lutetium do
Its noble gases are elements 2, 12, 22, 50, 78 and 138, each a peak of the first ionization energy
claims.value: noble gases 2, 12, 22, 50, 78, 138; each above both neighbours: yes

claims.claim: The hardest-held electron in the table isn't a noble gas's: element 128, whose 18-electron d shell is full with nothing outside it (our palladium's kind), out-holds its row's noble gas 138, and element 68, the same kind a row up, comes within a volt of its row's noble gas 78 (in ours palladium holds far less hard than xenon, 8.3 against 12.1 eV)
claims.value: 128: 29.56 eV (5p8 5d18) against 138: 26.71; 68: 22.32 eV (4p8 4d18) against 78: 23.10; the table's highest is element 128

claims.claim: The table's numbers are converged in the solver's stop: tightening it a hundred-thousandfold moves no total or ionization energy by a microhartree, nor Σ⟨r²⟩ by 10⁻⁴ of itself
claims.value: 19 atoms, both worlds: |ΔE| ≤ 2.7e-7, |Δion| ≤ 2.8e-7 hartree; Σ⟨r²⟩ ≤ 1.9e-5 relative, the bake's against the tight 7.0e-5

claims.claim: The table's ionization energies don't depend on the radial grid: halving or doubling its points, or moving either end by a factor of ten in or out, moves none by a millihartree
claims.value: 11 atoms, both worlds, six grids: |Δion| ≤ 1.4e-4 hartree; total energies ≤ 6.7e-2

claims.claim: 4D hydrogen comes out exact: −Z²/2(n + ½)² hartree, so −2/9 for the ground state
claims.value: -0.22222 hartree against -0.22222

claims.claim: The same solver in our three dimensions gets 32 of our 36 ground configurations
claims.value: 32 of 36; missed Ti, V, Co, Ni (one d electron too many against 4s: local exchange leans to d)

claims.claim: … and our first ionization energies to a few percent
claims.value: median error 4.3 %, largest 16.2 %

claims.claim: The rows are the geometry's, not the law's: solved with the shell theorem forced on, the first 24 elements keep every configuration, and the noble gases close the same rows at 2, 12, 22, 50, 78 and 138
claims.value: with the shell theorem: 1–24 unchanged (all settled, all the same); every atom to 88 settled; noble gases 2 same, 12 same, 22 same, 50 same, 78 same, 138 same. 28 atoms of row 6's f block don't settle under the shell theorem (89–116), so whether row 6 splits is open

claims.claim: The law decides what fills inside the rows: of the atoms settled under both, every change of configuration begins at the first d element, and under the shell theorem p beats d (element 25 takes 4s² 4p¹ where the law gives 3d¹ 4s²)
claims.value: 112 settled under the shell theorem; 57 differ, the first at 25; in every one the law's own configuration stays lower under the law (checked)

claims.claim: Element 128's hold on its outermost electron is the law's: with the shell theorem forced on it falls from the table's highest to a few volts, and the noble gases hold hardest, as ours do
claims.value: 128: 3.10 eV with the shell theorem against 29.56 under the law; the shell theorem's five highest are 12, 22, 50, 78, 138

claims.claim: Across the table the law holds outer electrons about two and a half times harder than the shell theorem would, and up to ten times
claims.value: first ionization, the law over the shell theorem, 110 atoms past helium settled under both: median 2.54, from 1.06 to 9.55

claims.claim: In ours every open subshell of the table has its maximum spin lowest (Hund's first rule), from the subshell's own repulsion
claims.value: 23 subshells (p and d) of our 36 atoms: all hold

claims.claim: In four dimensions Hund's first rule fails for d² and d¹⁶ in every d row, and holds for every other p and d filling of the table
claims.value: 82 p and d subshells; fails: 26 3d2 by 0.396 eV, 39 3d16 by 0.767 eV, 54 4d2 by 0.296 eV, 66 4d16 by 0.580 eV, 114 5d2 by 0.357 eV, 126 5d16 by 0.628 eV

claims.claim: … and so does its mirror 4f²⁹, three short of a full f shell: spin ½ again
In four dimensions 4f³ breaks it too: its ground term has spin ½

Why: two d electrons' terms have energies F⁰ + a₂F² + a₄F⁴ exactly; in 4D the ten-state singlet keeps the electrons nearer right angles than any triplet (⟨cos²γ⟩ 1/8, half of random) and lies lowest whenever F⁴/F² < 5/3, which every real orbital meets; in ours ³F is lowest for every F⁴/F²
claims.value: 4D: singlet ⟨cos²γ⟩ 0.125, best triplet 0.1875 (random 0.25); singlet lowest for F⁴/F² < 1.6667; element 26's F⁴/F² 0.391 (1/r), 0.650 (Gauss). Ours: ³F 0.2245, ¹D 0.2925 (random 1/3); ³F lowest for all F⁴/F² ≥ 0: true

claims.claim: The failure is the 4D shell's, not the law's: Gauss's 1/r² gives d² the same singlet ground term, further below its triplet
claims.value: element 26's orbital: triplet above the singlet by 0.3961 eV under 1/r, 0.8231 eV under 1/r²

claims.claim: Resolving the terms changes no ground configuration: it lowers the eight Hund-breaking atoms' energies and moves eight first ionizations by 0.3–0.7 eV; the wider search behind it finds one configuration the bake missed (element 82: 4f¹ 5d¹ 6s², our cerium's kind)
claims.value: 92 elements searched again; configurations changed by the terms: none; by the wider search: 82 (5s2 5p8 6s2 → 5s2 5p8 5d1 6s2, -0.363 eV); ionizations moved: 54 6.41→6.71, 55 8.28→7.91, 66 18.82→19.40, 67 20.56→19.93, 114 6.92→7.27, 115 9.28→8.83, 126 24.92→25.55, 127 27.23→26.56

claims.claim: In ours the solver's misses have one cause, a bias toward d: moving a 4s electron into 3d comes out too cheap in every 3d atom measured, by about a volt; resolving the open subshells' whole term structure doesn't remove it, and gets fewer configurations right
claims.value: 4s→3d, solver against measured (eV): Sc 0.138 vs 1.4269, Ti -0.894 vs 0.8058, Fe 0.509 vs 0.8749, Co -0.346 vs 0.4171, Ni -1.155 vs -0.0298; mean error -1.048, with the full term correction -1.052; configurations right 28 (bake) and 26 (full correction) of 32

claims.claim: Atomic response, converged: the coupled response gives hydrogen exactly and our closed-shell atoms within about 10 % of reference values (alkalis and alkaline earths too polarizable); in four dimensions the permanent pull C5 = 3Q²/64 outranges dispersion everywhere outside the atom except for hydrogen, helium and the alkali-like atoms
claims.value: 27 atoms; quadrature 2 × 10⁻⁶, grid 0.5 %, sum rule ≥ 0.90; ours' median error α 9 %, C6 13 %; R* (bohr): H, He 28 and 9.26, s-like 4.9–94, the rest 0.59–1.5

claims.claim: 4D's d² singlet survives a ligand field on the axes at every strength, gives way to a triplet only narrowly at the tesseract's corners, and the 24-cell doesn't split d at all; ours' d² keeps its triplet
claims.value: axes: ground singlet at every s (last 1×2); corners: triplet from Δ 2.4707 eV; 24-cell spread 0; ours' grounds true, true

claims.claim: Stretched pairs of light atoms come apart into neutral atoms with their own spins in both worlds; in 4D the separated limit of closed-shell atoms is the permanent pull −3Q²/64R⁵, which Hartree–Fock reproduces
claims.value: pairs ours H₂, N₂, F₂, Ne₂, 4D 1, 2, 7, 10, 11, 12: charges below 10⁻⁵, ours' interaction at 16 bohr ≤ 0.001 mHa; 4D at 16 bohr, Hartree–Fock over the far form: closed 1.02–1.06, H 1.15, open p 1.4–1.9; basis error closed 0.00 to 6.60 mHa

claims.claim: Valence states: one-electron moves from the ground by both methods; on ours the Rydberg moves hold to a few tenths of an eV, and the s→p promotion of an atom with its p shell under half full is too cheap in both methods
claims.value: 33 calibration states; Rydberg medians 0.4 and 0.3 eV; s→p (Be, B, C, Mg, Al, Si) −2.3 to −0.6 (local exchange) and −1.7 to −0.9 (Hartree–Fock); 4D 2s→2p of element 4 1.3 and 1.5, darbon 3.4 and 4.0 eV

claims.claim: The valence rule tested on one hydride: darbon's DH₅, with the five bonds the rule counts, is a true minimum (every curvature in four dimensions positive) and lies below both balanced alternatives, DH₄ + H and DH₃ + H₂, each fragment in its lowest spin
claims.value: 24 coordinates, 10 rigid, 14 curvatures in groups 5 + 4 + 1 + 4, lowest 0.020 Ha/bohr², none negative, gradient 0.00000459; DH₅ → DH₄ + H 1.551/2.321 eV, → DH₃ + H₂ 2.135/3.433 eV (Hartree–Fock/MP2)

claims.claim: A second method, numerical Hartree–Fock, on the same candidates: in ours it gets more ground configurations than local exchange, and where the two agree they are right; its 4s→3d promotion errors change sign at half filling, so the two methods don't bracket the measured value. In 4D the two agree on most of the table, and the rest are open

Our lanthanides calibrate Hartree–Fock on the f row: it makes f too stable in every measured state that changes the f count, by at most B ≈ 4 eV. In 4D, f is bound so deeply that over half of row 6's f block is firm against that bias; the open cases sit at the block's two ends
claims.value: lanthanides: Hartree–Fock 15, local exchange 12 of 18; f too stable in 17 of 17, by 0.15–4.1 eV; f out of the ground: 90 5.8, 100 12.6, 109 19.9 eV, Tb 0.9 (measured 0.04); firm 81, 88–100 and 102–104; open though agreed 82 (1.53 eV), 84 (0.40), 85 (1.12), 86 (2.21) and 87 (3.86); leaning Hartree–Fock 83 and 107–111; untested 101, 105, 106 and 112

claims.claim: The 4D shell kernel has a closed form, κ(t) = 4[(1 + t²)E(t) − (1 − t²)K(t)]/3πt² in complete elliptic integrals, with κ(1) = 8/3π and κ = 1 − t²/8 − t⁴/64 − …
claims.value: closed form against the solver's quadrature at t = 0.1 … 0.9: largest relative difference 2.7e-15; at t = 1: 0.848826 against 8/3π = 0.848826

claims.claim: In ours, searching each ion for its own ground state changes no ionization; the anion search gets every unbound anion unbound and every p-block acceptor bound, and fails only where correlation does the binding (H⁻, the alkalis, P and As)
In 4D, seven ions rearrange when searched for their own ground states, lowering those ionizations by up to 1.3 eV; element 128's is unchanged
One electron short of a full 4D p shell, atoms hold an extra electron harder and harder down the group, where ours hold it about equally: partial screening again
claims.value: p⁷ electron affinities (eV): 11: 3.39, 21: 5.71, 49: 7.81, 77: 10.25, 137: 12.88; ours (2p⁵, 3p⁵, 4p⁵): F 2.80 (measured 3.401), Cl 3.15 (measured 3.613), Br 3.01 (measured 3.364)

claims.claim: Without a shell theorem outer electrons are held much harder than shell-theorem screening allows
A neutral atom pulls on a distant electron as −Σ⟨r²⟩/8s³
